claims.statement: Choose Go constructs by semantic clarity and explicit ownership; reference-bearing values crossing a trust or lifetime boundary must expose whether storage is borrowed, transferred, shared under synchronization, or independently copied.
claims.scope: Go language, declarations, data structures, errors, interfaces, generics, naming, and memory ownership
claims.invariant: A maintainer can determine value ownership, mutation, failure, and control flow from the local API, and no retained or returned alias permits uncontracted mutation, lifetime extension, or concurrent access.
qualifications: The Go specification defines validity, not house style.
Existing public APIs and repository conventions can outweigh a local preference.
Copying is conditional on ownership, trust, and lifetime; a synchronous borrow need not allocate when retention and mutation are excluded.
A full slice expression narrows append authority but does not create independently owned storage.
counterexamples: Changing an established exported name solely to satisfy a style preference can be a compatibility regression.
A pointer is not automatically preferable for a large value when identity and mutation are not part of the contract.
Cloning only an outer map can retain aliases to mutable slices in its values.
Returning a buffer to sync.Pool while an asynchronous consumer retains it transfers live storage to an unrelated task.

claims.statement: Put dependency seams at behavior boundaries owned by the consumer, and introduce abstraction only when it isolates a real variation or failure boundary.
claims.scope: Packages, modules, interfaces, dependency injection, constructors, and project layout
claims.invariant: Core behavior can be exercised without importing transport, storage, or process bootstrap details.
qualifications: Small concrete dependencies are often clearer than interfaces.
A repository layout is not an architecture by itself.
counterexamples: A one-implementation interface created beside its implementation can add indirection without isolation.
Framework-specific applications may reasonably follow framework layout at the outer boundary.

primary_evidence.title: Go Wiki: Code Review Comments - Interfaces

claims.statement: Version a public Go module from its complete consumer-visible source and behavioral contract, and prove a major-version cutover from external consumers rather than from the producer repository alone.
claims.scope: Exported Go APIs, module paths, release versions, toolchain requirements, errors, defaults, ownership, serialized data, configuration, and consumer migration
claims.invariant: A supported consumer can select, import, compile, and exercise the candidate without an unannounced source, identity, behavioral, wire, or operational break; incompatible v2+ packages have a distinct /vN module path and can coexist with the preceding major.
qualifications: The Go 1 compatibility promise governs future Go language and standard-library releases, not every third-party module or external protocol.
Semantic versioning communicates the intended boundary but does not prove compatibility.
A type alias preserves type identity, not every constructor, error, side effect, import, or support commitment.
counterexamples: Adding a method to an exported interface breaks external implementations even though the producer repository still compiles.
A local go.work or replace directive can hide an invalid module path or incomplete published artifact.
Adding an exported struct field can break unkeyed external literals or change encoding behavior.

primary_evidence.title: Go 1 and the Future of Go Programs

claims.statement: At HTTP, gRPC, GraphQL, and OpenAPI boundaries, validate once, preserve protocol semantics, bound work, and keep domain behavior independent of transport encoding.
claims.scope: Network service APIs and adapters
claims.invariant: Malformed, canceled, oversized, duplicated, partially written, or generation-crossing requests cannot bypass domain invariants or leave uncontrolled work or connection state behind.
qualifications: Protocol-specific status and retry semantics must remain visible at the adapter.
Streaming APIs require lifecycle handling beyond request-response handlers.
A versioned client cutover must preserve one captured policy and transport generation per admitted operation while retiring obsolete idle resources without interrupting in-flight work.
counterexamples: Converting every domain failure to HTTP 500 or gRPC Unknown destroys retry and client-correction semantics.
Mutating an in-use transport or swapping policy separately from its client can make one operation observe two configuration generations.

claims.statement: Select deterministic tests, fuzzing, race detection, static analysis, and integration checks from the failure modes a change can introduce, not from a fixed test template.
claims.scope: Go testing and automated verification
claims.invariant: Each material invariant has an executable oracle at the cheapest layer that can falsify it.
qualifications: Race detection observes executed paths and cannot prove the absence of all races.
Fuzzing is most useful with fast deterministic targets and meaningful invariants.
testing/synctest virtualizes time and quiescence only for its owned bubble; external I/O and outside goroutines need separate fakes or integration evidence.
counterexamples: A table-driven test is not inherently better than direct tests for a single behavior.
Mock call-order assertions can freeze implementation detail without validating behavior.

claims.statement: Establish a reproducible workload and profile the dominant resource before optimizing Go code; report both effect size and cost transfer.
claims.scope: CPU, allocation, memory, contention, scheduling, I/O, and latency diagnostics
claims.invariant: An optimization improves the target production constraint without violating correctness or moving an unacceptable cost elsewhere.
qualifications: Microbenchmarks require stable setup and statistical comparison.
Profile-guided optimization does not replace end-to-end latency and capacity evidence.
The Go soft memory limit covers runtime-managed memory rather than process RSS; binary, cgo, mmap, and operating-system memory require measured headroom.
counterexamples: Replacing readable code with allocation tricks before identifying allocation pressure can reduce maintainability with no material gain.
Setting GOMEMLIMIT equal to a container hard limit and forcing memory return periodically can add continuous GC cost while leaving external memory unbounded.

primary_evidence.title: A Guide to the Go Garbage Collector

claims.statement: Treat every external input, credential, dependency, generated artifact, and privileged operation as a trust boundary with explicit validation, least privilege, and failure containment.
claims.scope: Application, supply-chain, authentication, authorization, cryptography, and secret handling
claims.invariant: Untrusted data cannot acquire authority merely by reaching an internal type or generated path.
qualifications: Security controls must follow a threat model and deployment context.
Use maintained cryptographic protocols and libraries rather than custom primitives.
Forwarded and client-certificate headers acquire authority only from an authenticated, non-bypassable proxy path that sanitizes attacker-supplied fields and owns the interpreted hop chain.

Envelope encryption makes routine KEK rotation a rewrap only when the DEK and data construction remain acceptable; DEK compromise, excessive key use, or algorithm and format migration can require re-encrypting data.
Old key destruction requires decryptability and retention evidence across live data, replicas, queues, backups, recovery, and rollback paths; scan completion alone is insufficient.
counterexamples: Input validation alone cannot repair an authorization decision made at the wrong resource boundary.
A syntactically valid X-Forwarded-For or Client-Cert value supplied through an unauthenticated or direct backend path is attacker-controlled metadata, not transport identity.
Rewrapping a leaked DEK under a new KEK preserves the compromised data key, while destroying the old KEK before backups and rollback readers migrate can make retained data unrecoverable.

claims.statement: A Go service owns startup validation, readiness, bounded shutdown, telemetry continuity, deployment evidence, and rollback safety as part of its public production contract.
claims.scope: Configuration, logging, metrics, traces, health, shutdown, containers, Kubernetes, CI, and releases
claims.invariant: The process never advertises readiness before it can serve safely, does not abandon accepted work without an explicit shutdown policy, does not let telemetry failure create unbounded work, and does not treat replica progress or binary rollback as proof of application or data correctness.
qualifications: Readiness and liveness probe semantics depend on orchestration and failure-recovery strategy.
Deployment progress and availability describe platform reconciliation, not complete business correctness or data compatibility.
Rollback restores only the resources covered by the deployment mechanism and may be unsafe after new data, messages, configuration, or irreversible effects.
Telemetry must remain bounded and avoid sensitive or high-cardinality dimensions.
Dropping or sampling telemetry can be safer than blocking, but loss, saturation, and sampling must themselves be observable through an independent bounded path.
counterexamples: A liveness probe that fails on every downstream outage can turn a dependency incident into a restart storm.
An unbounded exporter queue can turn collector failure into process memory exhaustion while an unlimited flush can defeat the shutdown budget.
A Kubernetes Deployment can be Available while a canary violates a financial invariant, and rolling back its Pod template does not undo database writes or an external ConfigMap change.

primary_evidence.title: Kubernetes Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes

claims.statement: Every goroutine needs a bounded creation rate, an owner, a completion condition, and an explicit error, panic, cancellation, and shutdown contract; shared memory requires a documented synchronization relation.
claims.scope: Goroutines, channels, mutexes, atomics, worker pools, supervision, panic isolation, and context propagation
claims.invariant: Load, cancellation, panic, or partial failure cannot create unbounded live goroutines, unobserved terminal failures, unsafe resource release, or unsynchronized conflicting memory access.
qualifications: Not every goroutine needs its own context when ownership provides a stronger completion mechanism.
Channels and mutexes solve different ownership problems; neither is categorically superior.
WaitGroup.Go is available in Go 1.25 and later, carries no error result, and requires that its function not panic.
Recover is valid only in the panicking goroutine at an intentional isolation boundary where safe continuation is established.
counterexamples: A process-lifetime telemetry goroutine can be owned by process shutdown rather than a request context.
A defer in a parent goroutine cannot recover a panic in a worker goroutine.
Logging a recovered panic and restarting with partially mutated state is not supervision.

claims.statement: Choose transaction boundaries, isolation behavior, and read authority from the business invariant; make the full read-check-write effect atomic and never infer write outcome from a weaker read.
claims.scope: SQL transactions, isolation, locking, optimistic concurrency, replica reads, cache consistency, pagination, and online data changes
claims.invariant: Every committed outcome, correctness-dependent read, and mixed-version migration state satisfies the domain invariant under permitted concurrent executions.
qualifications: Isolation names do not guarantee identical behavior across database engines.
Serializable transactions may require safe retries and do not make external side effects transactional.
Online migrations are mixed-version protocols whose DDL locks, rewrites, validation, and failure artifacts must be verified for the deployed engine version.
Replication durability acknowledgement and replica query visibility are separate contracts; PostgreSQL remote_apply semantics do not establish a portable database rule.

Keyset pagination removes OFFSET position shifts only relative to a deterministic total order; mutable sort keys can still duplicate or omit rows, and a stable cross-request snapshot requires an explicit retained data version.
counterexamples: Read Committed can be sufficient for independent predetermined row updates but unsafe for cross-row invariants implemented as read-then-write.
An offset-paginated unconditional backfill can skip rows and overwrite newer writes while still reaching an apparent final page.
A row absent from an asynchronous replica after primary commit is a stale observation, not proof that the transaction rolled back.
A base64 cursor containing only a non-unique timestamp is neither a total-order boundary nor protection against tenant, filter, or sort tampering.

claims.statement: Assume messages can be duplicated, delayed, reordered, or redelivered unless the complete broker-consumer-state boundary proves stronger semantics.
claims.scope: Queues, logs, consumers, outbox/inbox, acknowledgements, ordering, and poison messages
claims.invariant: Redelivery, quarantine, redrive, or crash at any acknowledgement boundary cannot violate the business invariant or silently lose required work.
qualifications: Exactly-once features are scoped to particular systems and transaction boundaries.
Global ordering is expensive and usually unnecessary; identify the ordering key.
Dead-letter movement and redrive can change broker identity, enqueue time, retention, and relative order; preserve application identity and treat replay as a controlled release.
A consumer-group generation or member epoch may reject stale offset progress without fencing an external business effect already started by the revoked owner.
A CDC bootstrap needs a source-consistent snapshot and retained stream boundary plus collision handling; the exact snapshot, position, and watermark primitives are connector-specific.
counterexamples: A broker transaction cannot make an arbitrary third-party API side effect exactly once.
Emptying a DLQ at maximum velocity can interleave old and new events, outlive deduplication retention, and reproduce downstream overload.
A Read Committed table scan followed by the current log head can lose writes committed during the scan, while last-arrival-wins can let an older snapshot row overwrite a newer stream event.

claims.statement: Retry only operations whose duplicate effects are safe, within one end-to-end deadline and retry budget that accounts for amplification across layers.
claims.scope: Timeouts, cancellation, retries, circuit breaking, load shedding, and backpressure
claims.invariant: Recovery traffic cannot exceed the capacity reserved to recover, and a caller never interprets an ambiguous side effect as a known failure.
qualifications: Backoff with jitter reduces synchronization but does not create capacity.
A circuit breaker is useful only when its state and fallback semantics match the dependency failure mode.
counterexamples: Retrying at client, proxy, and service layers can multiply attempts even when each layer uses a small retry count.

primary_evidence.title: AWS Builders Library: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

claims.statement: Treat leases, elections, and regional promotion as time-bounded authority evidence; protect irreversible effects with an application generation, fencing, or storage-level conditional writes.
claims.scope: Leases, leader election, distributed locks, regional writer failover, coordination recovery, sagas, and multi-service recovery
claims.invariant: A delayed, partitioned, or restored former owner cannot commit an effect after a newer application generation has taken over, including across regional promotion and failback.
qualifications: Consensus-backed services reduce but do not remove client pause and stale-owner hazards or fence effects outside their state machine.
A restored coordination snapshot is a new logical lineage whose counters may not order application authority against surviving old writers.
Sagas provide compensating workflow, not ACID rollback across services.
counterexamples: Mutual exclusion inside one Go process can use a mutex and does not require fencing tokens.
DNS steering can move new traffic while a former region continues queued or external work.

primary_evidence.title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm

claims.statement: Represent money with an explicit currency and exact integer minor units or an exact decimal whose scale and rounding policy are part of the operation contract.
claims.scope: Monetary amounts, currency metadata, conversion, allocation, and rounding
claims.invariant: Stored and transferred amounts are exact under the selected currency exponent, every lossy conversion names its rounding rule, and every booked FX result is reproducible from persisted rate and allocation evidence.
qualifications: Not every currency uses two decimal minor units.
Some products require sub-minor precision or non-currency units; preserve the original scale separately.
Currency metadata cannot select a commercial rate, spread, quote lifetime, accounting accounts, tax stage, or jurisdictional rounding policy.
counterexamples: Binary floating point can be appropriate for analytics where exact settlement values are not produced, but not for ledger postings.
Summing signed numeric amounts across unlike currencies can appear to net to zero while proving no valid accounting balance.

claims.statement: Record immutable balanced journal entries with explicit accounts, currency, economic effective time, posted and recorded time, and external correlation; correct history through linked replay-safe journals and derive balances from postings or a transactionally consistent projection.
claims.scope: Double-entry ledgers, journals, balances, reversals, corrections, temporal views, and audit history
claims.invariant: For each journal and currency, signed debits and credits net to zero; committed history changes only through compensating entries, and correction replay preserves both the current effective view and any promised known-at historical view.
qualifications: Account normal-balance conventions must be defined by the ledger model.
A high-throughput projection may be authoritative only if its rebuild and reconciliation semantics are explicit.
The applicable accounting policy determines materiality, closed-period handling, retrospective restatement, authorization, and jurisdictional treatment.
Effective, posted, recorded, and source time names must be bound to product semantics rather than assumed to be universal accounting vocabulary.
counterexamples: A simple single-party stored-value counter may not need a general ledger, but then it cannot claim double-entry controls.
Changing a posted journal's amount or effective date can make a current balance appear correct while destroying historical and audit reproducibility.
Recomputing a reversal at the current FX rate or allocation policy creates new economics rather than undoing the original booking.

primary_evidence.title: Modern Treasury: How to Scale a Ledger
IAS 8 Basis of Preparation of Financial Statements

claims.statement: Model authorization, capture, refund, reversal, dispute, and asynchronous processing as explicit monotonic transitions driven by persisted provider evidence.
claims.scope: Provider or rail payment lifecycles whose current state contract has been verified; conditional modeling otherwise
claims.invariant: No transition invents a successful movement of funds, and late provider events remain safely applicable or explicitly quarantined.
qualifications: Provider state names and legal finality differ by rail and region.
A locally terminal state can still receive chargebacks or settlement adjustments.
Stripe evidence supports Stripe behavior only; it does not establish ACH or other rail idempotency, query, expiry, finality, dispute, or fee semantics.
Partial capture, void, authorization reversal, and unused-hold release semantics must come from the verified provider and payment-method contract.
A dispute is an independent amount-bearing case with its own identity, evidence deadline, decision, and funds events; multiple partial disputes can reference one payment.
counterexamples: Treating an HTTP timeout as a declined payment can trigger a second successful authorization.
A refund, customer withdrawal message, or local deadline timer does not by itself prove a Stripe dispute was won or that funds were reinstated.

claims.statement: Bind an idempotency key to the authenticated operation identity and canonical request, serialize concurrent first use, persist the business outcome atomically, and reject mismatched reuse.
claims.scope: Money-moving commands, API retries, provider calls, webhooks, and replay
claims.invariant: Any number of equivalent retries produces at most one committed financial effect and returns an outcome consistent with that effect.
qualifications: Retention must cover the maximum credible retry and replay window.
Provider key support, operation scope, account or region scope, retention, concurrent-duplicate behavior, and replayed response semantics are endpoint- and version-specific.
Provider idempotency does not replace local idempotency around local state changes or authorize disclosure of a stored result.
counterexamples: A check-then-insert implementation without a uniqueness constraint races under concurrent requests.
Reusing a provider key after its retention window or in a region outside its deduplication scope can create a new financial effect.
A simultaneous duplicate conflict can mean the first request is still processing rather than that no effect occurred.

claims.statement: Keep authorization, clearing, settlement, fees, reserves, and bank movement as separate evidence-bearing events rather than collapsing them into one paid flag.
claims.scope: Clearing, settlement, payout, reserves, and external account movement
claims.invariant: Every external movement and fee can be traced to immutable source evidence and its corresponding ledger postings.
qualifications: Rail-specific cutoffs, calendars, netting, and finality must come from the applicable scheme and processor contract.
Fedwire acceptance, cancellation, contingency reconciliation, and protracted-outage finality are specific to the active Operating Circular 6 and Regulation J contract.

For FedACH, a return is a separate value-bearing item, a Notification of Change is a nonvalue correction message, and a reversal is a narrowly permitted corrective entry; deadlines and permissions depend on active rules, code, account and entry class, role, calendar, and processing schedule.
counterexamples: A synchronous internal transfer within one ledger may settle atomically and need no external clearing state.
A missing Fedwire acknowledgment after a connection failure is not a rejection; an unreconciled contingency resend can produce a second accepted payment order.

FedACH forward settlement does not erase the original when a later return settles, while an NOC moves no funds and a generic reversal cannot serve as guaranteed cancellation after a timeout, suspected fraud, or funding failure.

claims.statement: Reconcile internal expectations to independently obtained external evidence by stable identity, amount, currency, and lifecycle, with explicit missing, duplicate, mismatched, and timing-break states.
claims.scope: Processor reports, bank statements, ledger projections, and operational exception queues
claims.invariant: Every normalized economic component belongs to exactly one currency-balanced 1:1, 1:N, or N:1 match group or remains a visible, owned exception; reruns and corrected artifacts preserve lineage and do not duplicate adjustments.
qualifications: Timing differences need aging policy and cutoff calendars rather than immediate adjustment.
Automated repair requires a stronger authorization boundary than automated detection.
counterexamples: Comparing only aggregate totals can conceal equal and opposite item-level errors.

claims.statement: Minimize payment-account and personal data at ingestion, isolate the cardholder-data environment, tokenize where possible, and make access and administrative changes tamper-evident.
claims.scope: Payment data, credentials, authentication, audit, retention, and compliance controls
claims.invariant: Sensitive authentication data and secrets never enter logs, generic events, idempotency keys, model or tool inputs, or lower-trust storage; reusable-token and detokenization access is attributable, purpose-bound, tenant-bound, and least-privileged.
qualifications: PCI DSS scope and regulatory obligations require a qualified assessment of the actual system and contracts.
This guidance is engineering support, not legal or compliance certification.
Tokenization narrows scope only according to the actual raw-data, token, key, routing, detokenization, support, backup, and administrative data flow.
counterexamples: Encryption without key isolation and access control does not remove a system from the trust boundary.
A service that tokenizes PAN but copies the raw request into a retry queue, trace, or support prompt remains in the sensitive data path.

claims.statement: Treat sanctions screening as versioned evidence feeding a qualified adjudication and financial-disposition workflow, never as an eternal clearance or an automated legal conclusion.
claims.scope: Risk-based sanctions screening, provider integration, candidate handling, holds, adjudication, rescreening, false-hit controls, evidence, and privacy
claims.invariant: Every disposition is attributable to the governing program, screened facts, list and provider evidence, policy version, qualified authority, and time; unknown or changed evidence cannot silently become clear, and retries cannot duplicate a hold, release, or economic effect.
qualifications: Exact screening scope, thresholds, timing, disposition, reporting, retention, and jurisdictional duties require current qualified legal and compliance interpretation.
Fuzzy-match scores are retrieval signals whose false-positive and false-negative trade-offs must be calibrated and tested under the actual risk program.
Fail-open, fail-closed, and manual-review behavior is a program decision, not a universal engineering default.
counterexamples: A provider timeout or partial response is not evidence that a party is clear.
A permanent name-only false-hit allowlist can suppress a changed list entry or different subject.
A low match score cannot itself authorize release of held funds.

claims.statement: Agent-skill performance claims require locked prompts and fixtures, isolated randomized arms, deterministic scoring before blinded semantic scoring, repeated uncertain cases, and raw artifact publication.
claims.scope: golangskills.com evaluation and release evidence
claims.invariant: A reported comparison can be reproduced from a named fixture, model/client configuration, grader version, and raw run artifact without treatment contamination.
qualifications: Same-platform model grading is labeled as such and is not independent human evaluation.
A failed leadership gate permits evidence publication but forbids a category-leadership claim.
counterexamples: One manually selected prompt and one run cannot establish general superiority.

claims.statement: Reference-repository branding, contributor workflow, generated files, and tool-specific process claims do not become canonical Go guidance merely because they occur beside a skill.
claims.scope: Competitor-specific repository mechanics
claims.invariant: Only material technical guidance and benchmark assertions enter domain adjudication.
qualifications: Packaging mechanics are compared separately when they affect discoverability or compatibility.
